models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: (Long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth) × NAV Rs 326.48: 0.76x / 1.06x / 1.74x book, with ROE 14% / 16% / 19% and growth 5% / 6% / 7%. Today's price implies a long-run ROE of about 14.7%.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: 2027 EPS Rs 55 / 63 / 70 × 4.5 / 5.5 / 6.5. The base is 14% below the reported Rs 72.96 run-rate because that includes the one-off tax credit; taxed normally the run-rate is about Rs 57.6, and the base adds 9% for a full year of the HSBC book. P/Es within the 2022–2025 range and below the justified 5.7x / 7.0x / 9.8x.

models.name: Dividend model
models.comment: Next year's dividend Rs 6.6 / 7.6 / 8.4 (12% of EPS, as now, counting the scrip half), growing 8% / 12% / 15% for five years (below the 19.2% supported), then 5% / 6% / 7% with the payout rising to 1 − growth ÷ ROE (about 63%). Most of the value comes after year 5, so this method rests on the bank paying out far more later.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Used instead of a cash-flow DCF, which doesn't suit a bank. Book Rs 326.48 plus profit above the cost of equity: ROE moves in a straight line from 19% (2026 with a normal tax rate) to 14% / 16% / 19% over ten years, 12% payout, then the excess return grows at 5% / 6% / 7%. The bull case is high because 88% of profit is kept and compounds; treat it with care.

summary.headline: A high-return bank below the buy price after buying HSBC's retail arm: Rs 304 against a Rs 323 buy price, but 2026 profit growth is a one-off tax credit and capital has thinned
summary.text: Nations Trust Bank (NTB.N0000) is a high-return niche bank (cards, premium retail, SME and corporate) that bought HSBC Sri Lanka's retail business on 1 May 2026. At Rs 303.75 (last trade on 30 September; the CSE close couldn't be fetched in this run) it trades at 0.93x group NAV of Rs 326.48 and about 5.3x trailing earnings taxed normally, below my buy price of Rs 323. Nine-month profit after tax rose 34% to Rs 20.0bn (EPS Rs 59.92), but that comes from a one-off tax credit tied to the acquisition: profit before tax was flat at Rs 21.8bn, and the third quarter fell 11% on Day 1 provisions and integration costs. Loans grew 35% in nine months, net Stage 3 is only 0.72%, but CET1 fell from 19.6% to 12.8% because the Rs 22.2bn of goodwill comes off capital, so the bank raised Rs 15bn of Tier 2 debt and proposes a Rs 13.9bn rights issue at Rs 305. Fair value is about Rs 380 (about Rs 371 a share if the rights issue goes ahead). Buy up to Rs 323; Rs 285 or less is a strong buy. Main risks: the HSBC book's credit quality, thinner capital, goodwill to be split into intangibles that will be amortised, and a provisional beta.

notes.disclaimer: These are estimates from the 2025 annual report and the 2026 interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, the HSBC acquisition accounting is provisional, the beta is provisional, and the price is the last trade of 30 September 2026, so check the current price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.

Decision box.Verdict: Buy: Rs 303.75 (30 September) is 20% below fair value of Rs 380 and below the Rs 323 buy price. Check the current CSE price first.
Decision box.Expected yearly return at Rs 303.75: About 17–20% a year if the price stays near 0.93x book: book growth of about 15–17% (88% of a 19% ROE kept, before the rights issue) plus a small cash dividend. More if the price moves towards fair value.
Decision box.Downside / upside: Bear case Rs 240 (−21%); bull case Rs 621 (+104%).
Decision box.What the price assumes: At 0.93x NAV, with 6% long-run growth and a 15.4% cost of equity, a long-run ROE of about 14.7%: far below the bank's 21–24% of 2023–2025.
Decision box.Confidence: Medium: P/B, P/E and the dividend model agree on Rs 347–372 (base); residual income is higher (Rs 403). The HSBC numbers are provisional, 2026 profit is flattered by tax, and the beta is provisional.
Decision box.Margin of safety: Yes at Rs 303.75: about 20% below fair value; Rs 285 or lower is a strong buy.

Business and moat.What it does: A mid-sized Sri Lankan commercial bank (95 branches, 2,880 staff) with consumer, commercial and corporate banking. It is the sole issuer and acquirer of American Express cards in Sri Lanka, the market leader in credit cards, and strong in premium banking; it now owns HSBC's former retail business.
Business and moat.Moat: Narrow but real: the Amex franchise and card leadership, a premium customer base and the industry's lowest net Stage 3 ratio. Banking is competitive and regulated.
Business and moat.Growth: Net loans grew 50% in 2025 and 36% more in nine months of 2026 (partly the HSBC book); capital, not opportunity, is the limit.

Accounting quality.Underlying earnings: H1 2026 had a one-off tax credit tied to the HSBC acquisition (Q2 tax was a Rs 3.5bn credit; the amount of the one-off isn't separately disclosed). Taxed at the 2025 rate, twelve-month EPS to September would be about Rs 57.6 against Rs 72.96 reported (my estimate).
Accounting quality.Acquisition accounting: Rs 22.2bn of provisional goodwill; card, core-deposit and depositor intangibles are being valued, and will be amortised through profit once split out, with deferred tax.
Accounting quality.Trading and exchange: Trading gains (Rs 5.9bn) and other operating losses (−Rs 4.9bn) largely offset each other (exchange revaluation and hedges); read them together.
Accounting quality.Group vs bank: Bank profit includes a Rs 1.8bn dividend from subsidiaries; the group figures, used here, exclude it.

Sri Lanka checks.Interest rates: Watch: FVOCI bond losses cut equity by Rs 6.7bn in nine months; deposit costs are rising faster than loan yields (NIM 5.40% from 6.05%).
Sri Lanka checks.Rupee: Watch: a third of deposits and over a quarter of loans are in foreign currency.
Sri Lanka checks.Tax and regulation: Risk: VAT and SSCL on financial services (Rs 5.8bn in nine months) on top of income tax; the Banking Act requires John Keells and Central Finance groups to cut voting stakes to 15%.
Sri Lanka checks.Dependence on the state: Watch: about Rs 281bn of debt securities (FVOCI and amortised cost).

Crisis stress test (2022-style).What happened in 2022: Group impairment Rs 13.8bn against Rs 3.7bn in 2021; profit still rose to Rs 7.2bn; the share fell to Rs 46 (0.30x book); the dividend was paid only in shares.
Crisis stress test (2022-style).Today: A repeat with CET1 at 12.8% and an unseasoned card book would probably mean no cash dividend, possible further capital raising, and the price could halve. The bank would very likely stay profitable.

Investment case and sell rules.Why own it: A bank earning 19–24% on equity with the industry's best asset quality, bought at about book value, with the HSBC deal adding scale in its strongest segment.
Investment case and sell rules.The case is broken if: ROE (normal tax) falls below 15% for a full year, net Stage 3 rises above 2.5%, or capital forces another issue at a low price.
Investment case and sell rules.Sell triggers: Price more than 30% above fair value (above Rs 495); the case breaks; or a clearly better opportunity appears.

What this analysis doesn't cover: The CSE price feed couldn't be reached from this run; the price is the last trade at 30 September 2026.
Whether the rights issue was approved at the 16 November 2026 EGM isn't known from the reports read; valuation is per current share.
Damodaran's sector-beta pages and local beta pages couldn't be opened; only one local 5-year beta was found. Recheck in January 2027.
The size of the one-off tax credit isn't disclosed, so the normal-tax EPS of about Rs 57.6 is my estimate.
The 2024 annual report wasn't read, so last year's promises couldn't be checked; the promise tracker uses the 2025 report's plans.
Peer banks weren't compared in this run.

fullText:
Summary: Nations Trust Bank (NTB.N0000) is a high-return niche bank (cards, premium retail, SME and corporate) that bought HSBC Sri Lanka's retail business on 1 May 2026. At Rs 303.75 (last trade on 30 September; the CSE close couldn't be fetched in this run) it trades at 0.93x group NAV of Rs 326.48 and about 5.3x trailing earnings taxed normally, below my buy price of Rs 323. Nine-month profit after tax rose 34% to Rs 20.0bn (EPS Rs 59.92), but that comes from a one-off tax credit tied to the acquisition: profit before tax was flat at Rs 21.8bn, and the third quarter fell 11% on Day 1 provisions and integration costs. Loans grew 35% in nine months, net Stage 3 is only 0.72%, but CET1 fell from 19.6% to 12.8% because the Rs 22.2bn of goodwill comes off capital, so the bank raised Rs 15bn of Tier 2 debt and proposes a Rs 13.9bn rights issue at Rs 305. Fair value is about Rs 380 (about Rs 371 a share if the rights issue goes ahead). Buy up to Rs 323; Rs 285 or less is a strong buy. Main risks: the HSBC book's credit quality, thinner capital, goodwill to be split into intangibles that will be amortised, and a provisional beta.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 303.75, the last trade on 30 September 2026 (the CSE close couldn't be fetched in this run; the site replaces it with the daily close). 2026 range to September Rs 268.50–356.00. Non-voting NTB.X0000 Rs 385.25.
Nine months to September 2026 (group, unaudited): net interest income Rs 34.0bn (+18%), net fees Rs 8.3bn (+30%), total operating income Rs 45.3bn (+17%), impairment Rs 2.3bn (a Rs 0.4bn reversal a year earlier), costs Rs 15.4bn (+30%), profit before tax Rs 21.8bn (flat), income tax Rs 1.8bn (Rs 7.0bn), profit after tax Rs 20.0bn (+34%), EPS Rs 59.92 (Rs 44.72).
Third quarter: profit before tax −11%, after tax −28% (EPS Rs 13.26 against Rs 18.35).
Balance sheet: gross loans Rs 609bn, deposits Rs 676bn, NAV Rs 326.48, provisional goodwill Rs 22.2bn, CET1 12.80%, total capital 16.17%, net Stage 3 0.72%.
2025 (group): profit Rs 19.3bn, EPS Rs 57.76, dividend Rs 7.00 (half scrip), NAV Rs 293.12, ROE 21.86%.

The HSBC deal and capital
NTB bought HSBC Sri Lanka's retail business on 1 May 2026 for Rs 21.8bn in cash: about Rs 30bn of loans (Rs 20.6bn of it credit cards), Rs 132bn of deposits and Rs 104bn of cash. Nearly all the price is provisional goodwill (Rs 22.2bn), which is deducted from capital, so CET1 fell from 19.6% to 12.8%. The bank issued Rs 15bn of Tier 2 debentures in June and proposes a 3-for-22 rights issue of non-voting convertible shares at Rs 305 (Rs 13.9bn; EGM 16 November 2026). The June quarter carried a one-off tax credit tied to the acquisition, which is why 2026 profit after tax is up 34% while profit before tax is flat.

Required return
Cost of equity = 8.24% risk-free (12.24% bond less 4.0% default spread) + 0.70 beta × (4.2% + 6.08%) = 15.4%; bear 16.9%, bull 13.9%. The beta is provisional (Damodaran's money-center bank beta from a web-search extract; only one local 5-year beta, 0.18, was found).

Valuation table (Rs per share, before the rights issue)
Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted
Justified price to book | 246.9 | 347.3 | 567.8 | 361.3
P/E method | 247.5 | 346.5 | 455.0 | 338.5
Dividend model | 218.7 | 372.4 | 663.1 | 384.4
Residual income | 248.2 | 403.0 | 798.3 | 435.6
Average | 240.3 | 367.3 | 621.0 | 380.0

Fair value Rs 379.96; buy price Rs 322.97 (15% below); strong buy Rs 284.97 (25% below). With the rights issue at Rs 305, fair value per share would be about Rs 371.

Growth and earnings checks
Supported growth is 19.2% (87.9% of profit kept × 21.9% ROE); assumed growth 8% / 12% / 15% for five years stays below it because capital is the binding limit. The base 2027 EPS (Rs 63) is 14% below the reported Rs 72.96 run-rate because that includes the one-off tax credit; taxed at 2025's 32.2%, the run-rate is about Rs 57.6. The chosen P/Es (4.5 / 5.5 / 6.5x) are below the justified 5.7 / 7.0 / 9.8x. The dividend is small (12% payout, half in shares), so the dividend model depends on the payout rising after five years as growth slows.

Business tests: 3 of 4 pass (returns, capital, steady profit); the cash test fails on the low cash dividend. Category: buy now at Rs 303.75 (good business, price below the Rs 323 buy price).

Buy plan for 500 voting shares: 200 up to Rs 323, 150 up to Rs 305, 150 up to Rs 285; average about Rs 306, total about Rs 153,100. The 2026 low was Rs 268.50, so every tier is within this year's range.

Main risks: the acquired card book's credit losses as it seasons; capital (CET1 12.8%) and the rights issue; the goodwill being split into intangibles amortised through profit; falling margin (5.40%); the John Keells and Central Finance groups having to sell down to 15%; and the provisional beta.
